meta.title: Cantonese Jyutping and Tones
meta.subtitle: 39 tones, letters and endings · both directions, as two cards each
meta.desc: The first deck of the Cantonese collection, and a short one. Chinese characters are not an alphabet, so there is no script to learn before the words: the characters are taught where they belong, a word at a time, in the level decks. What every card in the collection does print is Jyutping, the Linguistic Society of Hong Kong's romanisation, and this deck is the key to it. First the six TONES, all on the one syllable si — si1 poem, si2 history, si3 to try, si4 time, si5 market, si6 matter — because in Cantonese the tone changes the word, and the digit at the end of every Jyutping syllable names it; then the syllables ending in p, t or k, which take only three of the six. Then the letters Jyutping spells unlike English: b, d and g are said without a puff of air (as in spin, stop, skin) and p, t and k with one; j is an English y; z and c are ts sounds; ng can begin a word; and the vowels yu, oe and eo are rounded vowels English lacks. The letters that sound as in English (f, h, l, m, n, s, w) are left out. Each card asks both ways — the spelling, then its sound; the sound, then the spelling — and gives one word that shows it, with its meaning, its IPA and a speaker button. Sources: the sounds are the standard description of Hong Kong Cantonese phonology, and the IPA follows from the Jyutping by the same standard correspondence; the example words' Jyutping and meanings are CC-Canto's and CC-CEDICT's (Pleco and MDBG, CC BY-SA).

fields.Sound:
tone 1: high level
high and level, at the top of the voice (some speakers let it fall a little)

tone 2: high rising
rising from the middle of the voice to the top, as an English question rises

tone 3: mid level
level, in the middle of the voice

tone 4: low falling
low and falling to the bottom of the voice

tone 5: low rising
rising from low to the middle of the voice

tone 6: low level
level, low in the voice, just under tone 3

checked syllables
a syllable ending in p, t or k stops short, the lips or tongue closing without a puff of air; it takes only tone 1, 3 or 6 (Cantonese grammars call these tones 7, 8 and 9)
